No Result View All Result Home News Politics Business Sport Football Health Entertainment Education Opinion Editorial Columns Others LeVogue Magazine Conferences National Economy Contact Us Hausa Edition Home News Politics Business Sport Football Health Entertainment Education Opinion Editorial Columns Others LeVogue Magazine Conferences National Economy Contact Us No Result View All Result No Result View All Result JUST IN: Tinubu Approves Establishment Of University Of Public Relations, Leadership by Samson Elijah 3 seconds ago in News Share on WhatsApp Share on Facebook Share on X Telegram President Bola Tinubu has approved the establishment of the University of Public Relations and Leadership, a specialised institution designed to advance education, research, professional development and leadership training in public relations and strategic communication.
Tinubu, who Vice President Kashim Shettima represented, announced the approval on Wednesday while addressing participants at the 2026 World Public Relations Forum (WPRF) in Abuja.
He described the proposed university as a first-of-its-kind initiative and a lasting institutional legacy of Nigeria’s hosting of the global public relations gathering.
The President said the institution would provide opportunities to develop a new generation of communication leaders equipped to respond to the demands of a rapidly changing global environment.
He commended the Nigerian Institute of Public Relations (NIPR), the Federal Ministry of Information and National Orientation, and the Nasarawa State Government for their collaboration and commitment towards making the vision a reality.
Tinubu urged relevant stakeholders to work together to ensure the university becomes a centre of excellence with national, continental, and international recognition.
He also called on public relations and communication professionals to uphold the highest standards of ethics, accountability, transparency, and responsibility, particularly in the face of growing misinformation and disinformation, and the challenges posed by artificial intelligence.
According to him, communication professionals have responsibilities beyond managing images and reputations, emphasising their role in promoting truth, accountability, mutual understanding, and constructive engagement among governments, institutions, and citizens.
The President said the Federal Government recognised the strategic importance of communication to national development, democratic governance, economic growth and international cooperation.
Tinubu further urged international delegates to explore Nigeria’s investment opportunities, entrepreneurial ecosystem, creative industries, cultural heritage and tourism assets.
He described Nigerians as confident, resilient and hardworking people, insisting that the country’s potential went beyond the negative narratives often portrayed on social media.
“Of the ten unicorns in Africa, six are in Nigeria: Flutterwave, Opay, Interswitch, Moove, Moniepoint,” he said.
He also highlighted Nigeria’s growing demographic influence, projecting that the country would have a population of about 440 million by 2050 and become the world’s third most populous nation.
The President further cited the achievements of Nigerians in business and the professional accomplishments of Nigerian immigrants abroad as evidence of the country’s human capital potential.
“The most outwardly mobile immigrant community in the United States is the Nigerian Americans. Sixty per cent of them have college degrees. So Nigeria goes beyond 419. Nigeria is much bigger than that,” he said.
He encouraged the delegates to engage with Nigerian institutions and businesses, establish professional relationships and explore opportunities for partnerships and investment.
“We hope that your experience here will encourage you to return, invest, collaborate, and become ambassadors of Nigeria’s positive story,” he said.
Meanwhile, African Ministers of Information have called for a coordinated continental communication framework to combat misinformation, strengthen public trust and project Africa’s voice globally.
The call emerged from a high-level roundtable on responsible communication where participants proposed stronger institutional cooperation, professional capacity building and regular consultations among African governments.
The Minister of Information and National Orientation, Mohammed Idris, said the proliferation of digital platforms and artificial intelligence had made credible and responsible communication a strategic governance priority.
Citing Nigeria’s experience with manipulated videos and misinformation, Idris warned that false narratives could distort public events, create panic and undermine confidence in government.
“Technology has come to stay. AI is here to help us if we use it properly. The challenge is to ensure that what we communicate is credible and honest,” he said.
The minister stressed the need to restore sustained cooperation among African information managers, recalling that the continent previously maintained platforms for collective engagement.
He proposed reviving the Annual Conference of African Ministers of Information to strengthen policy coordination and enable Africa to speak with a common voice on issues of shared interest.
“Collectively, we are stronger if we are united. There is a need to establish a robust system that enables us to look at Africa as one and speak with one voice once again,” Idris stated.
He also urged African countries to support Nigeria’s UNESCO Category 2 International Media and Information Literacy Institute in Abuja and strengthen collaboration among public media institutions, including the Nigerian Television Authority (NTA), Federal Radio Corporation of Nigeria (FRCN), News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) and Voice of Nigeria (VON).
“The Media and Information Literacy Institute is not just a Nigerian institution; it is a global opportunity. We should support it as part of a broader continental effort to promote media literacy, particularly among our young people,” he said.
Kenya’s Cabinet Secretary for Information, Communications and Digital Economy, William Kabogo Gitau, highlighted his country’s National Communication Policy, adopted in August 2026, as well as plans for a National Communication Centre to provide verified government information and facilitate citizen feedback.
He also advocated for professional regulation of public relations and stronger cross-border cooperation to combat misinformation.
“Trust between a state and its citizens is built through ordinary interactions: a question answered accurately, a service delivered as promised, and the same message from every part of the country. One government, one message, consistent,” Kabogo said.
Similarly, the Minister of Communication and Media and Government Spokesperson of the Republic of the Congo, Thierry Lézin Moungalla, called for a continental framework for ministerial consultations, professional training, public-private media partnerships and joint content production.
He emphasised that government communication must be integrated into the strategic machinery of governance.
“Government communication is no longer simply a public relations function. It must be strategic and structural, embedded in the framework of government administration,” Moungalla stated.
The Deputy Minister of Information, Publicity and Broadcasting Services of Zimbabwe, Omphile Marupi, highlighted his country’s 16 community radio stations and grassroots information structures as tools for inclusive communication.
He called for stronger media literacy, ethical journalism and African ownership of the continent’s narratives.
“We must communicate not simply to be heard, but to be understood. We must not only disseminate information, but also listen, engage and respond to the concerns of our people,” Marupi said.
The Chairman of the Information and Communications Committee of Ghana’s Parliament and Member of Parliament for Bunkpurugu Constituency, Abed-Nego Lamangin Bandim, advocated increased investment in government communication, expanded rural connectivity and improved welfare for journalists.
He disclosed that Ghana had earmarked 10 million Ghana cedis in its 2027 budget for journalists’ training, development and welfare.
“We cannot succeed with inadequate budgetary allocations for government communication. We must also ensure that journalists are properly supported and remunerated if we expect them to produce credible and independent information for our people,” Bandim said.
The roundtable ended with a shared commitment to strengthen continental communication cooperation, with Nigeria indicating its readiness to host the next meeting of African Ministers of Information.
